Planetary intelligence is the capacity for AI to steer global energy systems within ecological limits, integrating renewables, storage, critical-mineral supply chains, and demand management so that innovation drives resilience and inclusive access.
 
This paradigm calls for digital systems that are distributed, operate within real-world resource constraints, and anticipate long-term impacts on energy security and equity. AI must strengthen the foundations of a just, reliable, and affordable energy transition - rather than increase fragility.
 
Already, AI data centers consume more electricity than 150 individual countries and could demand 6.6 billion m³ of water annually by 2027. The minerals powering this growth - lithium, cobalt, rare earths - are extracted largely from the Global South while most of the value accrues elsewhere. Unless guided by principles aligned with the concept of planetary intelligence, the Energy-AI nexus risks deepening these inequities.
 
The question is no longer whether AI will shape the energy transition - it already is. The real question is how to steer it so that the benefits, resources, and risks are shared fairly.

Financing the Blue Economy involves a combination of private and public capital, often channeled through specialized financial instruments like blue bonds and blended finance mechanisms. This includes integrating blue economy criteria into existing financial systems, supporting blue economy activities through targeted investments in sectors like sustainable fisheries and renewable energy, and using ocean-focused financial products such as blue bonds, debt-for-nature swaps, and impact investing. Achieving this, requires collaboration between governments, financial institutions, and corporations to establish clear standards, transparent governance, and a strategic shift in capital allocation towards ocean health and economic growth. 

In a recent article, Belinda Bramley points to the critical role of banks in encouraging and then enabling investors to finance Blue Economy initiatives. As an example, she points to Asian Development Banks new incubator, which supports sovereign and corporate borrowers who have plans to offer blue bonds. In a keynote address at an event in 2021, organised by the same bank, I was able to add insights based on my own experience.
Another example - still at a formative stage - is the World Bank's Blue Economy toolkit to establish a development framework that is clear and can be universally applied. Although the Blue Economy is still a relatively new concept, and potential investors remain wary of committing the very large sums that are called for, there are different ways in which banks can help to build confidence. At different levels - international, regional, national and local - and from different sources of capital.
Bramley believes that banks can help to release much-needed investment. If the Blue Economy is to achieve its undoubted promise, much will depend on the ability of banks to achieve this.

Over and above the actions of different financial agencies, there is the underlying issue of a disparity between rich and poor nations. This is a theme which recurs throughout this book, reflecting the fact that the fulfilment of Blue Economy aspirations will fall well short if there is not a correcting mechanism to enable all parts of the world to invest.
Different nations have fallen behind in economic development, often through no fault of their own, and it is in the interests of all to
provide a more level playing field. The Blue Economy will not be achieved without this kind of recognition .

It has never been more clear the role energy plays in both stabilizing crises situations and longer-term development. Extreme heat drives demand for cooling systems that prevent illness; shifting rainfall patterns make powered solutions like precision irrigation and desalination important for stable food and water systems. With sustainable energy, countries can protect and advance development gains across health, food and water systems, education, and jobs, particularly for those most vulnerable to climate impacts. 

From this year's flash floods in South Asia that destroyed energy infrastructure, to last year's droughts in Latin America and southern Africa that reduced hydropower capacity - the time to build resilience into energy systems is now.

It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sustainable energy can be a true lever for human development.
 
At a time when cooperation is under strain, sustainable energy remains one of the most powerful levers for progress - creating jobs, powering schools and clinics, advancing gender equality, and building resilience. Because in the end, the energy transition is never only about megawatts; it is about people and communities. Yet with 666 million people still without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking, we must rethink where and how we act. That is why three priorities stand out:
 
⚡️ Clean cooking at scale - 2.1 billion people still cook with polluting fuels. Scaling clean cooking is not just about energy access, it is about saving lives, empowering women, and protecting the planet.
 
⚡️ Development assessment for a just transition - A just transition means linking energy to jobs, health, education, and resilience, so every investment delivers tangible benefits for people and communities.
 
⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableEnergy #CleanCooking #AIforDevelopment

We often discuss the role of #AI in energy through percentage gains - efficiency improvements, cost reductions, predictive accuracy. But the real impact is structural: AI is enabling new market dynamics that redefine how energy systems are governed and financed.
 
The foundation is the data infrastructure: smart meters, sensors, and digital grids generate continuous insight into how electricity is actually used. This demand-side visibility creates a national load profile that can enable transformative opportunities,
 
Once governments can see real demand and private sector can act on this #data, new dynamics  emerge:
	•	Auctions can be designed around measured needs, defining clearer requirements for renewables, storage, and flexibility
	•	Investors can leverage data to lower risk and improve project bankability
	•	Markets gain credibility as public data limits discretion and reduces risk of corruption
But the same visibility that empowers can also expose vulnerabilities. Without strong governance, data monopolies, surveillance risks, and algorithmic bias could distort markets rather than open them.
 
The #energy transition will not be powered by new technologies alone, but by the intelligence and integrity of the systems that govern them. Discover how in the newest Sustainable Energy Bulletin 👉  https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe

What if the future of AI wasn’t measured only in breakthroughs, but also in its true environmental cost?
 
Global data centers consume about 460 TWh of electricity annually - around 1.5 % of global demand. The portion of this demand from AI is growing rapidly and could reach 85–130 TWh by 2030. If this trajectory continues, AI could emit up to 1.6 Gt CO₂e by 2035 even as its deployment in energy, food, and mobility offers potential avoidance of 3.2–5.4 Gt CO₂e annually.
 
Because #AI operates on land, water, and kilowatt-hours, its footprint is real, and growing. Unchecked growth risks worsening energy inequities: many regions already grapple with power shortages, yet AI infrastructure is concentrated in the Global North.
 
By redesigning AI to align with planetary boundaries, we can mitigate its impact:
⚡ Transition data centers to 100 % renewable energy with transparent sourcing.
💧 Innovate in cooling systems to minimize water use and recycle heat for communities
📊 Promote efficiency standards and “green AI” benchmarks to guide responsible innovation
🌐 Ensure equitable access so the Global South benefits from AI advances, not just bears the costs
 
At the same time we can leverage its system benefits:
+⚡ AI optimization has already improved renewable-grid efficiency, raising wind power’s market value by up to ~20 %.
+💧 AI-based forecasting now prevents climate damages worth up to $50 billion annually through early-warning systems.
+📊 Optimization in logistics and manufacturing has already saved over 3 million metric tons of packaging material since 2015.
+🌐 Expanding sustainable AI infrastructure can accelerate investment in low-carbon technologies, projected to require $2.4 trillion annually by 2030 in emerging economies. 
 
To explore this further, I invite you to read my latest collaborative illuminem  article with my colleague Stefano Pistolese : 👉 https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

It's been a couple of months of sabbatical so far. While I'm still doing a couple of things for Alameda Institute as needed, this time on official leave is allowing me to catch up on a lot of things and finalise some strategic aspects of my current research projects.

I'm working on three book manuscripts. Now that the edited collection on land connections and struggles in Palestine is almost done, I get to focus again on my original manuscript on ecological transitions from a Global South perspective (which is long overdue to my publisher at Grupo Planeta , but I promise will be worth the wait). In the meantime, I'm also revising the topic of my first book from 2019 for Grupo Editorial Record to provide an update on the status of political fragmentation in Brazil, something very necessary given the still constant threat to our democracy.

But I'd like to share some other things that are already out.

1. The special issue of NACLA report, which I co-edited with my friend and dear colleague Breno Bringel . Titled "Green Capitalism in the Americas", it presents excellent pieces of research on the threats of false solutions and the opportunities for just alternatives when it comes to climate change. Our introduction is available here: https://lnkd.in/dwGjwQ_d (A few articles are open access, but as a member of the NACLA editorial board, I also encourage people to subscribe, since we do put out great issues every year!)

2. I was invited to write this piece for The Break Down on the dilemmas faced by Brazil to really advance its climate leadership. Considering that, historically, our emissions come mostly from land use change and deforestation, caused by dispossession and aggressive monoculture practices by agribusiness, it is impossible to take our NDCs and pledges seriously while landowning class continues to wreak havoc, including by controlling our Congress. https://lnkd.in/eHw6mzFq (it's a beautiful issue too, I highly recommend it)

3. And while today I finish teaching my special course on Planetary Limits and Ecological Transitions, I turn my attention to prepping for the closing keynote of the "A climate for change: Towards just taxation for climate finance". I think we are very fortunate to host this event in Brazil at a time where brilliant people who have long constructed a path for tax justice are finally getting heard, both regarding climate financing and changes to our unjust tax system. If you want to really understand both the synergies and tensions between #GreenHydrogen and #Development, there are 3 outputs you MUST read. 

1. 'Development strategies for the green hydrogen economy in emerging economies' by Fabianna Bacil, Anthony Black, Marina Domingues, Jun Jin, Rasmus Lema, Glen Robbins, Sören Scholvin. Available here: https://lnkd.in/ezcHwRpS

2. The United Nations report 'Navigating currents of Green Hydrogen Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework', by UNDP & TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, authored by Riad Meddeb, Pavel Bilek and I.
https://lnkd.in/e63jWxgb

3. 'Dismantling green colonialism: energy and climate justice in the Arab region', a book edited by hamza hamouchene and Katie Sandwell, which focuses on the politics of green extractivism with detailed cases across the Arab world. https://lnkd.in/eJK3cC2U

All three pieces are quite complementary. The first focuses on the sectoral choices and strategies pursued by different countries (Brazil, Chile, China, and South Africa) and explains differences in policies and outcomes. The second one links green hydrogen with human development needs, across energy access, environmental degradation and industrialisation, highlighting how developing nations can avoid the first mover disadvantage at the height the learning curve for H2.  The third one bring the political economy angle, the unevenness and dependencies that can created under current conditions and behaviours in green energy sectors, and provides cases that require careful examination with global relevance.

Green hydrogen can be a force for good or a terrible thing for humanity, developing nations and the planet. Whether it is one or the other will depend on how we collectively shape this agenda over the next decade.

Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Artificial intelligence is advancing at an extraordinary pace — opening a frontier that demands both imagination and responsibility. On one hand, AI holds immense potential to reshape our world. On the other, Earth’s life-support systems — climate, biodiversity, and water — are under unprecedented strain, and meeting these challenges will require ever more energy.

Global energy demand grew by 2.2% in 2024 — nearly double the recent decade’s average — with electricity consumption jumping by 4.3% as electrification, heat waves, data centers, and digitalization surged. Over the 2025–2027 period, electricity demand is expected to keep rising at around 3.9% annually.

In 2024, AI consumed 415 TWh of electricity — more than 150 individual countries. By 2030, global data center demand could reach 945 TWh, exceeding Japan’s total electricity use. Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live without reliable access to energy.

This poses an important question: what kind of intelligence are we building? Can AI learn from nature to design future energy systems that deliver a just transition?

In a reflection co-authored with Riad Meddeb , we explore the idea of Planetary Intelligence — the integration of human, technological, and natural systems to sustain habitable conditions.

Synchronize energy with the planet’s balance - AI can move beyond optimizing data centers to orchestrate energy flows as nature does — cutting grid losses, balancing renewables in real time, reducing emissions by up to 10% by 2030, and unlocking 175 GW of additional transmission capacity.

Integrating planetary health into our energy systems for smarter societies - When designed to mirror natural systems, AI can help manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity — generating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while preserving the ecosystems that sustain life.

Advancing an inclusive and equitable energy future -  From tracking bird migrations around wind farms to developing over 40 African language models, AI can amplify diverse voices and ensure that the energy transition becomes not only smarter — but also fairer and more resilient.

If AI is trained on the principles that govern life on Earth, it can help us see both the forest and the trees — guiding us toward an energy future that is more intelligent, more just, and more human.

Read more about planetary intelligence in our recent publication on Illuminem: https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB

From New York Climate Week to Building Bridges, Geneva — and onwards to COP30, Belém

At the 2025 #UNGA and #ClimateWeek in New York, I was struck by the growing momentum around real solutions—those that can transform lives and protect our planet.
Among the most overdue breakthroughs: clean cooking is finally on the global agenda.

At the #SDG7ActionForum, Sheila Oparaocha of #Energia and Heather Adair-Rohani from #WHO reminded us that “clean cooking” barely captures the grim reality of dirty cooking:
- 3.2 million premature deaths every year, mostly women, more than malaria, TB, and HIV combined.
- Girls and women are risking violence while spending hours collecting firewood.
- Families trapped by the cost of charcoal, LPG, or kerosene.
- Devastating health impacts, deforestation, and biodiversity loss.

As Riad Meddeb of #UNDP noted, the case for clean cooking is undeniable:
- Dirty cooking drains US$1.4 trillion annually in health and productivity losses.
- Only 1% of clean-energy investment targets clean cooking.
- 2.5% of global greenhouse emissions come from dirty cooking, the same as the aviation sector.

There’s no reason for this to continue. The technology exists—the missing ingredients are political will and financing at scale.

At #bloomberg hosted event Mary Schapiro, Catherine McKenna, María Mendiluce reminded us of the power of women in leading for climate change. Women-led innovation should answer the call of 400 million women to access clean cooking solutions. 

As Åsa Skogström Feldt of IKEA and Yasmina Zaidman of Acumen said at #ActionSpeaks, community engagement and trust are the catalysts that make social change unstoppable, but it takes time.

Enter CleanStove.org. We are proving that the future of clean cooking is community-led, off-grid, solar-powered, and battery-driven induction: ruggedized, reliable, smoke-free, and sustainable.

Each CleanStove® enables unlimited cooking in daylight, plus up to four hours after dark, with built-in LED lighting, USB charging, and eSIM-enabled smart monitoring. The feedback from women using pilot stoves in India, Senegal and Tanzania says it all: “It's a miracle”. 

At #BuildingBridges in #Geneva, another critical link emerged: clean cooking and high-integrity carbon credits. At CleanStove®, we’re enabling verified data from every stove—uploaded and secured in Switzerland—to generate real, traceable carbon credits, converted into direct cash transfers to women who cook.

Impact finance and philanthropy both play crucial roles. CleanStove® is building partnerships to make flexible payment models—such as pay-as-you-go, leases, or loans—accessible to base-of-pyramid households.

As we head toward COP30 in Belém, Brazil, let’s make clean cooking for all not just a climate goal — but a human right.

Our Global #MultidimensionalPoverty Index 2025 with the Oxford Poverty & Human Development Initiative (OPHI), University of Oxford is out NOW. 

This new research finds that of 6.3 billion people in 109 countries, 1.1 billion are multidimensionally poor.

Poverty is still our greatest global challenge, which is also a challenge compounded by the climate crisis.

Of the 1.1 billion multidimensionally poor people, 887 million live in regions which are exposed to at least one of four climate hazards: high heat, drought, floods, and air pollution. 

Many poor people face overlapping climate hazards. 651 million live in regions exposed to two or more of these climate hazards, and 309 million in regions exposed to three or four climate hazards.

As climate hazards continue to grow in frequency and intensity, countries which currently have higher multidimensional poverty levels will likely experience greater average temperature increases. It is vital to align poverty reduction efforts with climate action. In the face of the climate crisis, our commitment is clear: no one must be left behind.

*A Conservation Success Story: The Resilience of Sea Turtles*

Sea turtles have long fascinated humans with their ancient lineage and majestic presence in our oceans. However, their numbers have been declining due to various threats, including overconsumption, bycatches, pollution, and habitat destruction. Nevertheless, the story of sea turtles on Aldabra Atoll in Seychelles offers a beacon of hope, demonstrating that with protection and conservation efforts, it is possible to reverse declining trends and rebuild populations. Let's explore this remarkable conservation success and the lessons it holds for protecting our planet's precious wildlife.

*A Story of Resilience and Conservation*

On Aldabra Atoll, protective measures introduced in 1968 have yielded impressive results, with over 15,000 egg clutches recorded annually between 2014 and 2019. This represents a staggering 500% increase since the 1960s, with an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 green sea turtles visiting the beaches each year to lay eggs. 

The Aldabra experience showcases the effectiveness of local conservation efforts, which can make a real difference in protecting species, while also highlighting the need for national agreements and international regulations to address broader threats.

“Energy resilience” is not a uniform concept - it reflects distinct structural realities across regions and context.

🔵 In many crisis settings, it refers to continuity under disruption - distributed solar and storage systems keeping essential services operational amid physical and cyber risks.

🟠 In Central Asia, it implies interdependence - regional power pools projected to reduce generation costs by 8 percent through shared reserves and cross-border balancing.

🟢 In Sub-Saharan Africa, it denotes reliability - systems that can sustain demand growth and climate stress while extending access to those still excluded.

🔴 In Latin America and the Caribbean, it means protection - coastal grids redesigned with underground cabling and wind assets certified for category-five storms.

Yet, less than 1 percent of global adaptation finance is directed toward energy systems, despite investments in resilience returning multiples in gains in avoided losses and productivity.

Energy resilience binds infrastructure to governance, data to finance, and technology to social stability. In development terms, it is the capacity of an energy system to maintain function, equity, and trust when the environment around it changes.

Across Africa, the energy revolution is accelerating. Investments in renewables have nearly tripled since 2019, and solar is now the least-cost source of power in most African markets.

This transformation holds immense opportunity. Africa possesses around 60% of the world’s best solar resources, yet only 1% of installed solar capacity. Unlocking this potential could power homes and industries, create over 3 million new green jobs by 2030, and drive inclusive growth from the ground up. But for this revolution to deliver lasting development impact, it must be just - anchored in governance, innovation, and digital empowerment.

1️⃣ Strengthen Governance
Establish transparent, accountable institutions with continent-wide standards for procurement, land use, and revenue sharing to ensure renewable wealth translates into jobs, community benefits, and public trust.

2️⃣ Mobilize Innovative Finance
Move from isolated projects to bankable investment pipelines. Blended finance, risk guarantees, and local-currency mechanism can de-risk markets and crowd in private capital. By mobilizing the estimated $190 billion per year needed by 2030, African countries can power inclusive industrialization and deliver universal energy access.

3️⃣ Harness Digital, Data & AI
Leverage AI and digital tools to make systems smarter and more affordable. Predictive analytics can cut project costs by 15%, and generative AI - if locally embedded in value chains - could unlock over $100 billion in annual economic value.

Africa’s energy revolution is not a story of scarcity but one of sovereign opportunity. With the right governance, finance, and digital backbone, the continent can transform its renewable wealth into sustainable development and true energy independence.

Powershoring Finance in the Northeast of Brazil (2/3)

Building on the first round of the roundtable, this second discussion on Powershoring Finance in the Northeast of Brazil focused on the crucial role of national and subnational development banks (NDBs) in implementing financial mechanisms on the ground — opening new markets, taking on risks that commercial banks often avoid, and driving sustainable development where it matters most.

It was an honor to represent UNDP, through the Sustainable Energy Hub and the LAC EE Team, and to exchange ideas with Bruno Gabai (BNB) and Marcelo Saintive (BANDES), two key leaders in regional development finance.

💡 Key takeaways:
- Development banks have development in their DNA — they are uniquely positioned to combine financial innovation with territorial impact, supporting the green reindustrialization of the Northeast.
- We explored how to blend market-based instruments and business models with development outcomes such as job creation, social inclusion, technological advancement, and climate action.
- Subnational sovereign funds can play a pivotal role in decarbonization initiatives, for instance through the structuring of Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDCs) — a strong example of the financial innovation mindset of NDBs.
- Development impact tools are essential to design financial instruments that maximize socio-economic and environmental benefits, supporting sustainable infrastructure and powershoring.
- Constitutional and development funds, such as FNE and FDNE, remain vital sources of financing for the region’s transformation.
- National and subnational development banks can amplify their impact by channeling sovereign and non-sovereign operations from International IFIs through their structures, combining these resources with sustainable PPPs, concessions, and thematic bonds to finance powershoring and resilient infrastructure in the region.

This roundtable brought together an exceptional group of partners from international and national institutions — including UNDP, IFC, CAF, BNB, BANDES, SUDENE, FUNBIO, UnB, and ICS — under the umbrella of the event “How to Scale Up and Accelerate Sustainable Investments in the Northeast of Brazil: The Powershoring Opportunity.”

A big thank you to Banco do Nordeste (BNB), Consórcio Nordeste (CNE), and ICS for the kind invitation and continued collaboration.

Globally, renewable-power capacity is projected to increase by around 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030. The opportunity now is to ensure our digital, data, and human systems can absorb this growth—by strengthening coordination, governance, and skills to drive the structural change required for a just energy transition.

Today during Day 2 of the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I moderated a discussion centered on how digitalization, data, and AI can help overcome these limits—and the new vulnerabilities they create.

1️⃣ First, the main bottleneck for renewable adoption is now absorption capacity. Grids cannot integrate trillions of USD of investment in renewables without parallel investment in #digital coordination, data systems, and human expertise. If a solar panel lacks a sensor, it effectively doesn’t exist to the system.

2️⃣ Second, #AI must remain a decision-support system, not an autonomous agent. Human oversight and digital skills are essential—especially as clean-energy jobs now account for more than half of the world’s 67 million energy-sector jobs.

3️⃣ Third, a just energy transition requires algorithmic justice. Without inclusive data governance and intentional design, algorithms trained on developed grids will reinforce the very access gaps they could help close.

4️⃣ Fourth, flexibility remains the cheapest untapped resource. Yet, fragmented regulation still blocks dynamic tariffs and peer-to-peer trading. Digital tools can help realign incentives for consumers to use energy when renewables are abundant. Unreliable grids could otherwise cost developing economies $1.3 trillion in lost output by 2030.

Ultimately, the digital, #data, and AI revolution must serve human development. These tools are already creating new market dynamics that are redefining how energy systems are governed and financed, but we need to always be vigilant to preserve our focus on what actually matters: people.

#DigitalTransition #EnergyTransition #AIForEnergy #IFESD

⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewable investment reached USD 624 billion, yet less than 15 percent reached developing economies outside China — and only 2–3 percent to Africa. 

The task ahead is not just to mobilize more capital, but to unlocking opportunities for clean energy where the need and potential are greatest. That requires financial and institutional systems capable of structuring, verifying, and absorbing investments at scale.

At the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, leaders from across regions agreed: capital follows credibility. A few ways they converged on we can do this:

1️⃣ Build national financing ecosystems, not fragmented projects, that can enable bankability of projects.
Energy-efficiency funds in Kosovo, Jordan, and Moldova show these financial mechanisms. The key for bankability starts with structuring projects with clear revenue models, transparent governance, and measurable performance to minimize investor risk.

2️⃣ Aggregate small projects to match investor logic.
Commercial lenders seek diversification. Aggregating small clean-energy projects — solar rooftops, retrofits, micro-grids — into verified portfolios lowers risk premiums and opens new credit lines for municipalities and SMEs. Inclusion also remains the ultimate de-risking strategy, as funds led by women in risk-management roles have proven on average lower default rates.

3️⃣ Embed data integrity into all financial instruments as the foundation of credibility.
Accurate baselines, open performance data, and auditability are now prerequisites for green finance. In Africa, the @AFREC Energy Information System is helping lenders quantify risk and track national progress with greater confidence. Digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can accelerate access to finance — but ensuring the datasets they are built on are equitable remains central.

The real measure of progress will be how fast we can turn global liquidity into local legitimacy — through institutions capable of absorbing, managing, and sustaining capital.

Over the past days, Hurricane Melissa — one of the strongest Atlantic hurricanes on record, with wind speeds exceeding 300 km/h — has left behind devastating impacts across Caribbean’s islands, showing how climate vulnerability continues to define the frontline realities of many island nations.

Yet, amid destruction, there is also determination. Island states have long been global leaders in shaping the climate agenda — from calling for loss and damage as early as 1991, to now leading efforts toward 100% renewable energy by 2030. These ambitions are not just about technology or finance, but about shaping a different development model — one that is more inclusive, productive, and resilient.

I was pleased to represent UNDP virtually in the closing ceremony of the 10th GTI International Conference in Gozo, organized by Greening the Islands Foundation , to reflect with Edita Dranseikaite , Josianne Cutajar , Henk Rogers , camille dressler and moderated by Gianni Chianetta , on how island states can lead technologies built to resist climate vulnerabilities and inspire global solutions through a just energy transition: 

1. Integrating resilience and energy transitions.
 SIDS import around 90% of their energy as fossil fuels, often spending up to 10% of GDP annually. Transitioning to renewables could save up to USD 3.3 billion per year — roughly 3.3% of regional GDP — creating fiscal space to modernize ports, optimize grids, and strengthen essential services.

2. Financing resilience as an opportunity, not a cost.
 Every dollar invested in climate-resilient infrastructure generates about four dollars in avoided losses and economic benefits. Tailored financing mechanisms — from blended finance to de-risking instruments — can help island states attract investment while protecting communities from the next storm.

3. Harnessing digital and data intelligence.
 Digitalization is reshaping the way we plan, invest, and respond. Smart grids and AI can reduce energy losses (now equivalent to 1 gigaton of CO₂ annually) and unlock new efficiency gains.

A just energy transition is about ensuring that energy powers development across systems — water, food, health, and ecosystems. This is how island states can turn vulnerability into vision — not only bringing development to islands but bringing development from the islands. UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub Riad Meddeb

Last week, I had the opportunity to sit down with RASHID ABDALLAH, Executive Director of the African Energy Commission of the African Union  (AFREC), to discuss how data is reshaping Africa’s energy transition.

Data availability goes beyond merely monitoring progress; it plays a crucial role in de-risking investments and assisting governments and development partners in targeting projects and programs where they are most needed.

However, over 40 percent of African countries still depend on outdated or incomplete electricity data, which limits their ability to design effective policies or attract financing.

Since 2012, the African #Energy Information System, led by AFREC, has been enhancing the collection, validation, and dissemination of national energy data across the continent. Through capacity-building for national focal points, harmonization of data standards, and partnerships with regional and international organizations, AFREC is steadily improving the quality, credibility, and comparability of Africa’s energy data landscape.

In my discussion with Rashid, we explored how this initiative can align with UNDP ’s efforts to utilize geospatial analytics to move beyond binary indicators of energy access, aiming to understand how, where, and how effectively energy is used. After all, what does “access” mean if the energy is neither affordable nor reliable?

What innovations do you see as most promising for improving energy data availability? How can we ensure that #data-driven energy strategies translate into affordability, reliability, and equity?

🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt

It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries.
